## The idea

Go back to the workshop: 8 units of wood, 7 hours of labor, chairs earn 3 and tables
earn 4. Now a buyer offers to purchase **all** your wood and labor. She proposes a price
$y_1$ per unit of wood and $y_2$ per hour of labor. When would you accept?

You would refuse if some product earns more than the resources it uses are worth at her
prices: then you would rather build it yourself. So her prices must satisfy
$$
\begin{aligned}
y_1 + 2y_2 &\ge 3 && \text{(a chair's wood and labor are worth at least its profit)}\\
2y_1 + y_2 &\ge 4 && \text{(the same for a table)}\\
y_1, y_2 &\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
$$
She wants to pay as little as possible in total, $8y_1 + 7y_2$. That is another LP: the
**dual** of the workshop LP. Its optimum is $y^\star = (5/3,\ 2/3)$ with total payment
$18$, **exactly** the best profit you could make yourself. That equality is not a
coincidence; it is the strong duality theorem.

## The math

### The primal–dual pair

For an LP in the form
$$
\text{(P)}\qquad \max\ c^\top x \quad \text{s.t.}\quad Ax \le b,\ \ x \ge 0,
$$
the **dual** is
$$
\text{(D)}\qquad \min\ b^\top y \quad \text{s.t.}\quad A^\top y \ge c,\ \ y \ge 0 .
$$
One dual variable per primal constraint, one dual constraint per primal variable. The
roles of $b$ and $c$ swap, and $A$ is transposed. The dual of the dual is the primal
again.

For other forms, the rules are:

| Primal (max) | Dual (min) |
|---|---|
| constraint $a_i^\top x \le b_i$ | variable $y_i \ge 0$ |
| constraint $a_i^\top x = b_i$ | variable $y_i$ free |
| constraint $a_i^\top x \ge b_i$ | variable $y_i \le 0$ |
| variable $x_j \ge 0$ | constraint $(A^\top y)_j \ge c_j$ |
| variable $x_j$ free | constraint $(A^\top y)_j = c_j$ |

### Weak and strong duality

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (weak duality)
If $x$ is feasible for (P) and $y$ is feasible for (D), then $c^\top x \le b^\top y$.
:::

So any feasible dual solution gives an **upper bound** on the primal optimum, and any
primal solution gives a lower bound on the dual. In the workshop, the prices $y = (3, 0)$
are feasible for the buyer and show at once that profit can never exceed $24$.

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (strong duality)
If (P) has an optimal solution, so does (D), and the optimal values are equal:
$$
\max\{c^\top x : Ax \le b,\ x \ge 0\} \;=\; \min\{b^\top y : A^\top y \ge c,\ y \ge 0\}.
$$
:::

The duality theorem was first proved in print by @gale1951, using
[Farkas' lemma](../../foundations/polyhedra/farkas-lemma.qmd) [@farkas1902]. Together
with the [fundamental theorem](../modeling-and-geometry/geometry-of-lp.qmd), it leaves
only these combinations:

| | (D) optimal | (D) unbounded | (D) infeasible |
|---|---|---|---|
| **(P) optimal** | possible, equal values | impossible | impossible |
| **(P) unbounded** | impossible | impossible | possible |
| **(P) infeasible** | impossible | possible | possible |

The practical meaning: **an optimal $x$ always comes with a proof of optimality**, a
dual $y$ with the same objective value. Anyone can check it by verifying feasibility and
comparing two numbers.

### Complementary slackness

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (complementary slackness)
Let $x$ be feasible for (P) and $y$ feasible for (D). They are both optimal if and only
if
$$
y_i \,\big(b_i - a_i^\top x\big) = 0 \ \text{ for every } i
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
x_j \,\big((A^\top y)_j - c_j\big) = 0 \ \text{ for every } j .
$$
:::

In words:

- a resource that is **not used up** has price zero ($b_i - a_i^\top x > 0 \Rightarrow y_i = 0$);
- a product that **loses money** at the dual prices is not made
  ($(A^\top y)_j > c_j \Rightarrow x_j = 0$).

In the workshop both resources are used up and both products are made, so all four
conditions hold with equality, and $x^\star$, $y^\star$ can be found by solving two small
linear systems. Complementary slackness is also how an LP solver turns a primal solution
into dual values.

### The geometry: the objective lies in a cone

At the optimal vertex, the objective vector $c$ is a nonnegative combination of the
normals of the tight constraints, and the coefficients are exactly the dual prices.

::: {#cell-fig-optimality-cone .cell execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}

The objective $c = (3, 4)$ (green) lies inside it: $c = \tfrac53 a_1 + \tfrac23 a_2$ (dashed parallelogram). The coefficients are the dual prices $y^\star$. If $c$ were outside the cone, some direction along the boundary would improve the objective.](lp-duality_files/figure-html/fig-optimality-cone-output-1.png){#fig-optimality-cone width=459 height=469}

This is [Farkas' lemma](../../foundations/polyhedra/farkas-lemma.qmd) at work: either
$c$ is in the cone (and the dual multipliers exist), or a separating direction exists,
and that direction is an improving move for the primal.

## Why it works

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch: weak duality and complementary slackness
For feasible $x$ and $y$,
$$
c^\top x \;\le\; (A^\top y)^\top x \;=\; y^\top (Ax) \;\le\; y^\top b .
$$
The first inequality uses $x \ge 0$ and $A^\top y \ge c$; the second uses $y \ge 0$ and
$Ax \le b$. That is weak duality.

The gap $b^\top y - c^\top x$ is the sum of the two slacks
$\sum_j x_j\big((A^\top y)_j - c_j\big) + \sum_i y_i\big(b_i - a_i^\top x\big)$, a sum
of nonnegative terms. It is zero, which by strong duality is exactly optimality, if and
only if every term is zero. That is complementary slackness.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch: strong duality
Suppose (P) has optimal value $z^\star$. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, the system
"$Ax \le b$, $x \ge 0$, $c^\top x \ge z^\star + \varepsilon$" has no solution. Farkas'
lemma turns that infeasibility into multipliers $y \ge 0$ with $A^\top y \ge c$ and
$b^\top y < z^\star + \varepsilon$. Combined with weak duality, the dual optimum is
squeezed to $z^\star$. The details are written out on the
[Farkas' Lemma](../../foundations/polyhedra/farkas-lemma.qmd) page.
:::

## In practice

- **Solvers report dual values** (also called shadow prices or marginals) along with the
  solution. They are the subject of [Sensitivity Analysis](sensitivity-analysis.qmd).
- **The duality gap is a stopping rule.** Interior-point methods track primal and dual
  solutions together and stop when $b^\top y - c^\top x$ is tiny.
- **Decomposition runs on duals.** In
  [Benders decomposition](../../decomposition-methods/benders-decomposition/theory-and-mechanism.qmd)
  the cuts come from dual solutions of the subproblem; in
  [Dantzig–Wolfe](../../decomposition-methods/dantzig-wolfe/theory-and-mechanism.qmd)
  the master's dual prices tell the subproblems which columns to generate.
